opus-5.5.text:
I think compute constraints are probably the single most important factor people underrate when they talk about automating AI R&D. There's a popular story where you automate AI researchers, you suddenly have millions of copies of very capable researchers working on improving AI, and progress accelerates dramatically, maybe a software-driven intelligence explosion. My view is that this story leans too heavily on the idea that research progress is bottlenecked by researcher labor, when the evidence suggests experimental compute is at least as important, and probably more so.

If you look at how AI progress has actually happened over the past decade or so, much of it has come from scaling up compute, both for training the final models and for running the experiments that tell you which ideas work. Algorithmic progress is real and substantial, but it's not cleanly separable from compute. Many of the most important algorithmic insights only become visible, or only start to matter, at larger scales. You can't discover that something works at scale without running it at scale, or at least running a series of experiments that let you extrapolate.

So if you automate the researchers but the compute stock stays roughly fixed, you run into strong diminishing returns quickly. You have far more ideas being generated, but the same budget for testing them. Economists would say labor and compute are complements rather than substitutes. If the elasticity of substitution between them is low, and I think there's decent reason to believe it is, then massively increasing one input while holding the other fixed buys you much less than you'd naively expect. The researchers can be cleverer about which experiments to run, use smaller-scale proxies more efficiently, and avoid wasted runs, and that's worth something, but it doesn't make the compute constraint disappear.

Automated researchers also need compute to run themselves. If your AI researchers are running on the same hardware you'd otherwise use for experiments, there's a direct tradeoff: every copy of the researcher you spin up is compute you're not using to train or test models. That further weakens the case for a sudden, explosive feedback loop that's purely software-driven.

What I think is more plausible is that the big gains come when AI automates a much broader range of the economy, including chip design, fabs, energy production, and the physical infrastructure that produces compute. Then you get a feedback loop that grows the compute stock itself, not just the efficiency of using a fixed stock. That can still produce very rapid growth, potentially much faster than what we're used to, but it's a different, more gradual picture. It's tied to physical capital accumulation and the broader economy, not just a few labs automating their own research teams and taking off.

So my summary is that automating AI R&D will matter and will speed things up, but compute constraints mean the benefits are more modest and more spread out over time than the intelligence explosion picture suggests, unless you also scale up the hardware side, which brings in the whole economy.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose that each tenfold increase in effective compute automates an additional share of economic tasks.

r002.rationale: It argues that compute has driven much AI progress, so adding automated researchers while compute stays fixed leaves experiments compute-constrained and brings diminishing returns.

fable-5.1.text:
I think compute is the central constraint here, and it's the reason I'm more skeptical than a lot of people about how fast automating AI R&D actually pays off.

The intuition people often have is something like: right now AI progress is bottlenecked on the number of smart researchers at the frontier labs, so if you could run a million copies of a researcher-level AI, you'd get an enormous speedup. And there's something to that. But if you actually look at how research gets done at these labs, a huge fraction of the progress comes from running experiments. You have an idea for an architecture change or a data mixture or an optimizer tweak, and you don't really know if it works until you try it at some scale. And those experiments consume compute. So the labs are already, to a large extent, compute-constrained in their research, not just in their training runs.

Now, if you add a lot more researchers, whether human or AI, what happens? You get more ideas, you get better prioritization of which experiments to run, you probably get more careful engineering so you waste less compute. Those are real gains. But you don't get more GPUs. So the marginal value of an additional researcher is falling pretty quickly once you've got enough of them to saturate the available experimental compute. The returns to cognitive labor are diminishing when the complementary input is fixed.

The way I'd frame it is that there are really two factors going into AI progress: compute and labor, roughly. And historically they've grown together. Compute has been growing at something like four or five x per year in terms of training runs, and the labs have been hiring aggressively. When you automate R&D, you're essentially making labor very cheap and very abundant. But the elasticity of substitution between the two matters a lot. If they're close to perfect substitutes, then cheap labor can make up for scarce compute and you get a big acceleration. If they're complements, which I think is closer to the truth for a lot of the work, then you hit a wall where you're just waiting on experiments to finish.

There's another subtlety, which is that the AI researchers themselves cost compute to run. Inference isn't free. If you want to have the equivalent of a thousand or ten thousand researchers working in parallel, that's a nontrivial share of your cluster, and it's compute you're not spending on the experiments those researchers want to run. So there's an allocation problem within the lab: how much of your compute goes to thinking versus doing.

I don't want to be too deflationary about this, because I do think automation of R&D will matter. My guess is you get a meaningful speedup, maybe a factor of a few in the rate of algorithmic progress, rather than the kind of explosive, orders-of-magnitude acceleration that some of the more aggressive takeoff scenarios assume. And a lot of the actual acceleration would show up as better use of a fixed compute budget: fewer wasted runs, faster iteration on small-scale experiments, better extrapolation from small scale to large scale. Those are important but they're not unbounded.

The scenario where compute constraints bind less is one where AI systems get much better at making progress without large-scale experiments, through theory or through very good small-scale proxies. That's possible, and it would change the picture. But I don't think we have strong evidence that's how things will go, and the historical pattern in machine learning has been that empirical results at scale dominate.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose that each tenfold increase in effective compute automates an additional share of economic tasks.

r002.rationale: It argues that labs are already compute-constrained and that adding automated researchers does not add GPUs, so more researcher labor may not resolve the experiment-compute bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between automating the intellectual work of AI research and automating the entire process. If you have AI systems that can come up with good ideas and write the code to test them, that doesn’t mean you can run arbitrarily many experiments. You still need compute, and some experiments take a substantial amount of time.

So if you hold compute fixed and make research labor much cheaper, initially you might get a lot of benefit. You can explore ideas that researchers didn’t previously have time to pursue, analyze experimental results more carefully, and make better use of the hardware you have. But as you add more automated researchers, you would expect diminishing returns. At some point, you have many promising experiments competing for the same compute budget.

The important complication is that research can itself relax the compute constraint. If you discover a more efficient training algorithm, you can get a better model with the same hardware, or run experiments more cheaply. So there’s a potential feedback loop there. The question is how quickly you can find those improvements, and how much experimentation finding them requires.

That’s why I wouldn’t equate a thousandfold increase in research labor with a thousandfold increase in AI progress. You need to understand which parts of the research process are actually bottlenecked by people, which are bottlenecked by compute, and how those bottlenecks change as you automate more of the work.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not propose that each tenfold increase in effective compute automates an additional share of economic tasks.

r002.rationale: It explains that adding automated researchers does not remove a fixed compute constraint: more promising experiments compete for the same compute budget, even though research may sometimes improve efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between automating the research labor and automating the whole process of making progress. Even if you have AI systems that can generate ideas and write all the code, you still need compute to run experiments and find out which ideas actually work. So automating the researchers doesn’t necessarily mean you can speed up AI progress by an arbitrary amount.

But compute isn’t just a fixed barrier, either. Better research can make experiments more informative, or produce algorithms that use compute more efficiently. If AI researchers can find those improvements, you can get more progress out of the same hardware. The question is how much useful research can happen through thinking and small experiments, versus how much depends on running very expensive training runs.

So I’d expect substantial benefits from automating AI R&D, but the size of those benefits depends on where the bottleneck moves. If research labor is the main constraint, automation could have a very large effect. If compute is already the main constraint, adding more researchers has diminishing returns unless they can figure out how to use that compute better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute constraints and research automation, but does not propose that each tenfold increase in effective compute automates an additional share of economic tasks.

r002.rationale: It says that adding researchers may have diminishing returns when compute is the main constraint, but does not connect this to compute scaling having been the key driver of software progress.
